# Every positive-right-index double knot has negative envelope deficit

## Theorem and exact scope

Fix an integer d>=2, t=1/(d+1), theta=d/(d+1), and Gamma=theta^d.
Let integers H>=1, J>=1 satisfy

    J<=H,       H<=(2d+1)J+d.

At the double knot

    a=t(H+J+1)/[H(2J+1)],
    beta=t(H-J)/[d H(2J+1)],

For h ranging over the nonnegative integers, define r_h=(1-ah)_+,
q_h=t-beta h, p_h=t+beta(h+1), and the exact
diagonal envelope deficit

    D=Gamma sum_h r_h^d
       -d^d sum_h [q_h^(d-1)(r_h-dq_h)_+
                     +p_h^(d-1)(r_h-dp_h)_+].

Only positive-radius terms are included; hence q_h>0 whenever it is
used, and all sums are finite. Then

    D/Gamma <= -1/1080 < 0.                             (1)

This proves the full positive-right-index part of the double-knot
comparison in every dimension. It does not compare the remaining
J=0 knots, and it is not a general mixed-integer center theorem.

## 1. Scaled kernels and double-knot identities

Set

    v=(d+1)beta/a in [0,1],       b=d a v.

For x>=0 define

    L_v(x)=(1-vx)^(d-1)[1-(d+1-dv)x]_+,
    R_(a,v)(x)=(1+av+vx)^(d-1)
                     [1-dav-(d+1+dv)x]_+.

The left expression is used only on its nonnegative bracket support
and is set to zero elsewhere; its first factor is nonnegative there.
Let W=sum_h(1-ah)_+^d. Direct normalization gives

    D/Gamma=W-sum_h L_v(ah)-sum_h R_(a,v)(ah).           (2)

The left and right support endpoints are respectively aH and aJ.
In particular the right endpoint is an exact sampling point. Also

    1/[a(d+1)] = J+theta v(J+1),
    b = theta v/[J+theta v(J+1)],
    d a = theta/[J+theta v(J+1)],                       (3)
    b=(H-J)/[H(2J+1)] <=1/(2J+1)<=1/3.

These identities also hold at v=0, with b=0. Write

    A=1-b,       B=d+1+dv,       C=1+av.

Then R_(a,v)(x)=(C+vx)^(d-1)(A-Bx) on [0,aJ], and
aJ=A/B. All these expressions have positive denominators.

## 2. The exact trapezoid estimates

For a twice differentiable function on a mesh cell of width a, its
trapezoid error has the integral kernel
(x-left)(right-x)/2, whose maximum is a^2/8. The same formula holds
for a piecewise smooth function whose derivative has bounded
variation, by summing the cell formulas or integrating against its
second-derivative measure. Consequently a convex compactly supported
function f has

    0 <= sum_h f(ah)-(1/a)integral_0^infinity f-f(0)/2
       <=(a/8) Var(f').

For a concave smooth function ending at a mesh point where its value
is zero, the inequality reverses, with error bounded by
(a/8) times the decrease of its derivative on its active interval.

Apply the convex estimate to (1-x)_+^d. Its derivative changes from
-d to zero, so

    W <=1/[a(d+1)]+1/2+ad/8.                           (4)

The left kernel L_v is convex: on its active interval, both affine
factors decrease, and direct differentiation gives a nonnegative
second derivative. At the support endpoint its nonpositive derivative
jumps upward to zero. This includes the endpoint v=1, where both
factors vanish together. Since L_v(0)=1,

    sum_h L_v(ah) >=(1/a)integral L_v+1/2.              (5)

The right kernel is concave on its active interval: its second
derivative is

    (d-1)v(C+vx)^(d-3)
       [(d-2)v(A-Bx)-2B(C+vx)]<=0.

Indeed A-Bx<=C+vx, while B=d+1+dv. It vanishes at the exact mesh
point aJ. Its derivative decreases on that whole interval, so

    sum_h R_(a,v)(ah)
      >=(1/a)integral R_(a,v)+R_(a,v)(0)/2-E_R,         (6)

where

    E_R <=(a/8)[R'_(a,v)(0)-R'_(a,v)(aJ)].

There is no omitted support-endpoint cell: J is an integer.

Put Q=C+v aJ=1+av(J+1). The derivative difference in (6) is

    (d-1)v C^(d-2)A+B[Q^(d-1)-C^(d-1)]
       <=2(d-1)v A Q^(d-2).

The inequality follows from the mean-value bound for the positive
integer power. By (3),

    Q<=1+(J+1)/[d(2J+1)]<=1+2/(3d).

Hence Q^(d-2)<2. One elementary verification is
(1+2/(3d))^(d-2)<=exp(2/3)<2; the last strict inequality follows from
log 2=2 integral_0^(1/3)(1-s^2)^(-1) ds>2/3.
It follows, using A<=1 and (d-1)/d<=1, that

    E_R <= b/2.                                       (7)

All formulas include v=0, when this error is zero. At d=2, the
factor Q^(d-2) is one, so no differentiability issue is present.

## 3. The extra-shift integral loss

For 0<=s<=a let I(s,v)=integral_0^infinity R_(s,v)(x) dx, where

    R_(s,v)(x)=(1+sv+vx)^(d-1)[1-dsv-Bx]_+.

Throughout this segment 1-dsv>=1-b>=2/3. Its support endpoint is
positive, smooth in s, and bounded; the integrand vanishes there.
Thus differentiation under the finite polynomial integral introduces
no boundary value term. Writing C_s=1+sv, A_s=1-dsv, the exact
identity on the active interval is

    partial_s R_(s,v)=partial_x R_(s,v)
                         +(d+1)(C_s+vx)^(d-1).

For v>0, integration gives

    partial_s I
       =-C_s^(d-1)A_s
          +(d+1)/(dv)[(C_s+vA_s/B)^d-C_s^d].           (8)

Bernoulli's inequality bounds the difference in brackets below by
d C_s^(d-1)vA_s/B. Consequently

    partial_s I >=-C_s^(d-1)A_s *dv/(d+1+dv).

The factor C_s^(d-1)A_s is at most one: its derivative is
-v C_s^(d-2)(1+d^2sv)<=0 and its initial value is one. Thus

    I(a,v) >= I(0,v)-a*v/(1+v).                        (9)

For v=0, both integrals are identical and (9) is immediate. This is
an exact finite-shift estimate, not an asymptotic expansion.

## 4. Continuous gain and the endpoint contribution

The proved scalar theorem
`candidate 31c8bae81eb26cc3` gives

    integral L_v+integral R_(0,v)
        >=(1+v^2/4)/(d+1).                             (10)

Its hypotheses hold for every d>=2 and v in [0,1]. Combining
(4)--(10) in (2) yields

    D/Gamma <=-v^2/[4a(d+1)]+v/(1+v)
                  -R_(a,v)(0)/2+ad/8+b/2.             (11)

The own right kernel has the useful lower bound

    R_(a,v)(0)=(1+b/d)^(d-1)(1-b)
       >=(1+b/2)(1-b)=1-b/2-b^2/2,                    (12)

by Bernoulli and (d-1)/d>=1/2. Using (3), theta>=2/3, and J>=1,

    1/[a(d+1)]>=1+(4/3)v,
    b<=v/(1+2v),
    da<=1/(1+2v).

The quantities multiplying b in (11)--(12) are increasing for b>=0.
Substitution therefore gives the dimension-free upper bound

    D/Gamma<=U(v),

    U(v)=-v^2/4-v^3/3+v/(1+v)-1/2
           +3v/[4(1+2v)]+v^2/[4(1+2v)^2]
           +1/[8(1+2v)].                              (13)

No coefficient group, large dimension, large index, or limiting
approximation has been assumed in obtaining this bound.

## 5. Exact scalar positivity certificate

Clearing the positive denominator in (13) gives

    -U(v)=P(v)/[24(1+v)(1+2v)^2],
    P(v)=9+9v-60v^2-52v^3+88v^4+88v^5+32v^6.          (14)

Here is a complete rational certificate that P>=2/5 on [0,1].
For an interval [l,r], write v=l+(r-l)z and express the polynomial
in the degree-six Bernstein basis binom(6,j)z^j(1-z)^(6-j).
The seven exact coefficients, in increasing order, are:

* [0,1/2]:
  9, 39/4, 19/2, 317/40, 76/15, 43/24, 3/4.
* [1/2,3/5]:
  3/4, 13/24, 317/750, 2071/5000, 3377/6250,
  10353/12500, 20448/15625.
* [3/5,1]:
  20448/15625, 2019/625, 25726/3125, 457/25,
  13588/375, 331/5, 114.

These lists follow by direct expansion of (14). Each coefficient is
at least 2/5. The Bernstein basis is nonnegative and sums to one on
[0,1], so each list proves P>=2/5 on its entire interval. The three
closed intervals cover [0,1], including their common endpoints.

Finally 24(1+v)(1+2v)^2<=432 on [0,1]. Equation (14) gives

    U(v)<=-(2/5)/432=-1/1080.

Together with (13), this proves (1).

## Consequence for the remaining arithmetic comparison

After the previously proved compact-domain double-knot reduction and
the separately proved exclusion of escaping positive deficits, no
J>=1 knot can maximize a positive deficit. The only remaining knots
are J=0, hence beta=t/d, a=t(1+1/H), and 1<=H<=d. This note proves
their exclusion only when J>=1; it does not silently settle the
remaining finite-in-H, unbounded-in-d family.
